text: Someone assumes that if each person is careful, they're personally safe, but the real exposure isn't personal at all. It's shared. So, the real question, does five careful people add up to one safe team? Say four teammates each use Claude carefully on their own account. One adds a connector to read the shared team Dropbox. It's added at the account level, not just for that person. All four teammates' agents can now read every file in Dropbox, including a client contract marked confidential. No one intended this. No one knew. The natural guess, four people who are each careful with Claude, should add up to a team that's careful, too.

But nobody approved that connector for the whole team. Only one person clicked add for their own use. The account doesn't know the difference. The gap doesn't show up inside anyone's careful practice. It shows up at the boundary between people, in the shared space nobody owns. The shared folder was never anyone person's responsibility to fence. It belonged to all four accounts equally, which in practice meant it belonged to none of them. That doesn't mean every shared thing needs a rule. One teammate quietly reading their own files under their own login isn't a team-level risk. The fence only needs to go up around what's actually shared. Back to the four

Teammates, the fix was never asking anyone to be more careful. They already were. It's naming before anyone connects anything which data each agent can reach, who approves an account-level connector, and who's accountable if a client file leaks. That fence goes up around the shared space, not around any one person. Four careful people are not automatically a careful team. The team's safety lies in the fence around what they share, not in how carefully each person acts alone. Your turn. Here's the prompt. Read it with me. I'm setting up agent usage policies for a team of engineers who each use Claude responsibly on their own. Explain the team fence gap. What
